transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it's nice to meet you too, Doctor. I suppose what brings me in today is... well, it’s this whole situation with the local historical society. You see, I’ve been a member for years, mostly just attending the meetings and bringing a pie now and then, but recently they mentioned needing to raise funds for the old courthouse roof. And I just—I don't know, it was like a lightbulb went off, and suddenly I was taking on the entire fundraiser myself. I mean, I genuinely believed I could run the whole thing single-handedly. 

I started drawing up all these intricate quilt designs—because a raffle is always a good moneymaker, you know?—and I had fabric swatches spread out all over my dining room table, the living room floor, everywhere. Then I started calling all the volunteers, and I mean *all* of them, even people who hadn't been active in the society since the nineties. I was making these massive, color-coded schedules for everyone, assigning them tasks, and... and I was promising the board all these deadlines that, looking back now, I couldn't possibly meet. I told them we’d have three quilts done in a week and a fully catered gala planned by the end of the month. It was just... I was doing so much, and I felt like I had to do it all right that very second, and now it’s all just sort of crashed down on me.
During that time, did you feel unusually euphoric or on top of the world?

Well, yes, I suppose euphoric is a good word for it. At first, anyway. I felt... oh, I felt almost glowing, really. It was like every single idea that popped into my head was just absolutely wonderful, pure gold. I remember standing in the living room looking at all those fabrics—the calicos and the little floral prints I'd pulled out of the attic—and just feeling this incredible warm rush, thinking, 'I am going to save the courthouse, and it's going to be magnificent.' I felt so capable, so alive, like I was finally doing exactly what I was meant to do for the town and everything was just clicking into place perfectly. 

But then... well, you see, the trouble started when people didn't quite see the vision. If anyone questioned me—like Martha, she's the treasurer of the society, and she had the nerve to call and ask if maybe three quilts in a week was a bit too ambitious for our volunteer base—I just got incredibly snappish. I mean, unusually short-tempered for me. I snapped right back at her on the phone. I acted like she was deliberately standing in the way of progress, just dragging her feet to ruin my plans. I think I even told her that if she didn't want to help, she should just step aside because we had history to save and no time for doubters. I was just so intensely irritated that they couldn't keep up with how wonderful everything was, and it felt like they were all just intentionally trying to block me from getting this glorious project done.
About how many days in a row did that unusually energized and irritable period last?

Well, let me think back, because it all blends together when you're moving that fast, you know? I remember the leaves were just starting to turn when I first got the idea for the quilts, right around the time they put the pumpkins out at the grocery store. And then it just... it kept going. I was running on that high, just pushing and pushing through the holidays, through the new year, even into the early spring. So, goodness, that whole overdriven stretch with the historical society project went on for about five months, give or take. 

Five whole months of me just buzzing around like a bee trapped in a jar, making phone calls at all hours, reorganizing the fabric piles, arguing with Martha about the budget for the gala catering... I mean, I can hardly believe it went on that long when I sit here and say it out loud. But it did. Day in, day out, just this constant, humming energy and that terrible, prickly irritability every time someone couldn't match my pace. It wasn't until late March, maybe early April, that the bottom just completely fell out and everything fell apart. But for those five months, I was just... I was an absolute whirlwind, and I couldn't stop if I tried.
During that five-month period, were you ever hospitalized because of how energized or irritable you were?

Oh, no, no, I was never in the hospital for any of it. Goodness, the thought never even crossed my mind, and I don't think it crossed anyone else's either, at least not that they said to my face. I mean, where would I have even found the time to be hospitalized? I was much too busy! I had all those schedules, the fabric swatches, the caterers to wrangle... I suppose, looking back, people probably thought I was just being incredibly eccentric or maybe just a bit too passionate about local history. 

You know, my neighbor, Susan—she lives right across the street, lovely woman, always keeps her petunias looking so nice—she did come over one afternoon when I was dragging a massive roll of batting out of my trunk. She asked if I was feeling quite alright because I was talking a mile a minute about the courthouse roof and how we were going to have a silent auction with a Victorian theme. But even she didn't suggest a doctor or a hospital or anything like that. She just brought me a casserole a few days later and told me to remember to breathe. 

So, no, no hospital visits. I was just out there in the world, running around town, arguing with Martha at the bank, buying out the entire craft store's supply of rotary cutters... just living my life at a hundred miles an hour, completely unsupervised, if you can believe it. It's almost frightening to think about now, how I was just out there, spinning like a top for all those months, and nobody stepped in to stop me or take me to a clinic. But no, I managed to stay out of the hospital through the whole ordeal.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest in almost everything?

Well, let me think about that... depressed or lost interest. You know, it's funny you ask it just like that, because after all that rushing around with the quilts and the historical society—after that whole five-month whirlwind I was just telling you about—I did crash, like I said. The bottom just fell out. But... was it two weeks? Was it depression? 

I don't really know if I'd call it being depressed, exactly. Or maybe I would? It's so hard to put a label on these things when you're the one living inside them. I mean, I remember sitting in my armchair in the living room—the blue floral one, right by the window where the afternoon sun comes in—and just looking at all those leftover fabric scraps in the corner. Piles and piles of calico and gingham that I had been so obsessed with just days before. And I just... I didn't care about them anymore. The thought of sewing another stitch made me feel almost physically heavy. 

But as for it being a whole period of two weeks where I felt down or lost interest in everything... I'm really not sure. I mean, my daughter came to visit right around Easter, and we did go out to brunch at that little bistro on Main Street, and I think I enjoyed the mimosa and the eggs benedict. I don't remember feeling completely hopeless or anything like that. I was just so exhausted, you know? Like a balloon that had all the air let out of it. 

I stopped returning Martha's calls, of course, but that was mostly because I was too embarrassed about how I'd spoken to her before. And I stopped going to the society meetings. I just wanted to sit in my quiet house and watch the dust motes in the sunlight and not have to make any decisions about centerpieces or fundraising goals. But was it a true, deep depression that lasted for weeks on end? I really couldn't say for certain. It felt more like a terrible, lingering hangover from all that energy, just this profound tiredness where nothing seemed as shiny or important as it had before. So, I don't know if that counts as what you're asking about.
Before this five-month high-energy period, had you ever gone through a time when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Well, before that five-month period? No, no, not before. The timeline is... well, it’s all very specific in my mind because of how things played out with the historical society and the quilts. See, the really bad part—the part where I felt just completely awful every single day—that didn’t happen *before* the whirlwind. It happened *after*. 

It started right around the time I realized what a mess I’d made of everything. The orders for the quilts had fallen completely behind because I’d promised far too many to far too many people, and the volunteer conflicts... oh, they just blew up spectacularly. Martha and I had that terrible row over the catering budget, and then Susan got involved, and before I knew it, half the committee wasn't speaking to me. And when I finally stopped moving fast enough to see the wreckage, that’s when it hit me. 

And it didn't just last two weeks. Heavens, no. I’ve been stuck in this incredibly low, heavy, guilty place ever since. It’s been... goodness, it’s been about nine months now of just feeling utterly weighed down by it all. Nine whole months of waking up and feeling this pit in my stomach about the quilts I never finished and the people I snapped at. I just sit in that blue armchair and think about how I ruined the gala, and the days just bleed into one another. So, no, not before the high energy. But after? Yes, for nine long months, just feeling completely stuck in the mud.
